questions.q: Which question is a sliding-window problem?
questions.explain: "Run of consecutive" is the signal: the answer is a contiguous range. The other questions ignore positions (frequency counter) or search sorted data (binary search).
options: Are these two order lists the same, in any order?
What is the longest run of consecutive on-time deliveries with at most one late?
Which payment method is used most often?
Is order ORD-501 in this sorted list?

questions.q: How many different 7-day periods does a list of 30 days contain?
questions.explain: A period can start at day 1 up to day 24 (days 24 to 30 is the last one): n − k + 1 = 30 − 7 + 1 = 24.

questions.q: What does recomputing the sum of every window of size k cost on n values?
questions.explain: There are n − k + 1 windows and each costs k additions. With k = 720 hours over 43,800 hours that is about 31 million additions.
options: O((n − k + 1) · k), roughly O(n · k)

questions.q: The window over days 10 to 16 totals T. What is the total for days 11 to 17?
questions.explain: The two windows share days 11 to 16. Day 10 leaves, day 17 enters: one subtraction and one addition, whatever the window size.
options: It must be added up again

questions.q: How many operations does the fixed-size sliding window make on 43,800 hourly values with a 720-hour window?
questions.explain: The first window costs k, each of the remaining n − k slides costs one update: n in total, independent of the window size.
options: About 43,800: 720 to fill the first window, then one per slide

questions.q: A fixed window of size k ends at position right (inclusive). Where does it start?
questions.explain: Check a tiny case: k = 3, right = 3 covers positions 1, 2, 3, so it starts at 1 = 3 − 3 + 1. Position right − k is the one that just left.

questions.q: There are only 5 days of data and the owner asks for the best 7 days. What should bestPeriod return?
questions.explain: Returning the 5-day total silently answers a different question. Make the missing answer visible.
options: null (or an error): there is no 7-day period, and the report should say "not enough data"

questions.q: bestPeriod updates the best with if (total > best.total). Two periods tie for the highest total. Which one is reported?
questions.explain: Strict > keeps the first best; >= would keep the last. Choose on purpose and document it.
options: The earlier one, because an equal total does not replace it

questions.q: The revenue table has no rows for days the shop was closed. What goes wrong with a 7-row window?
questions.explain: Fill closed days with a 0 revenue row so that positions line up with days, or slide over dates (SQL RANGE with an interval) instead of rows.
options: 7 rows can span more than 7 calendar days, so "best 7 days" compares periods of different lengths

questions.q: In the "at most one late delivery" streak, the window just became invalid (two lates). Why can left move forward for good?
questions.explain: It is the same argument as in two pointers: each move discards a candidate that cannot win. That is why the window never needs to move backwards.
options: Because the right edge will move back later
Every window that starts at the current left and reaches this far contains both lates, so no longer valid window can start there
Because the first delivery is always late
It cannot; you must restart from right

questions.q: The variable window has a while loop inside a for loop. Why is it still O(n)?
questions.explain: Count total pointer moves, not loop nesting. This "amortised" argument is the key to every variable-window solution.
options: Because the while runs at most once per step
left only moves forward and never passes right, so across the whole run it moves at most n times; together with right, at most 2n moves
It is not; it is O(n²)

questions.q: A developer shrinks the streak window with if (late > maxLate) instead of while. What can go wrong?
questions.explain: The late delivery that must leave may be several positions in. Keep shrinking until the rule holds again.
options: Nothing; one step is always enough
One step left may remove an on-time delivery, leaving the window still invalid, so an invalid window gets recorded as a streak

questions.q: In the longest-block-without-repeat solution, why check previous >= left before jumping left?
questions.explain: With "abba", the last a's earlier position is 0 while the window starts at 2. Jumping to 1 would put both bs in the window.
options: The earlier play may already be outside the window; jumping to it would move left backwards and let a duplicate back in
Because Maps store positions in reverse

questions.q: prefix[i] is the total of the first i values, with prefix[0] = 0. What is the total of positions from to to, inclusive?
questions.explain: Everything up to and including to is prefix[to + 1]; subtract everything before from, which is prefix[from]. The leading 0 makes ranges starting at 0 work with no special case.

questions.q: When are prefix sums a better fit than a sliding window?
questions.explain: Build once in O(n), then answer each range in O(1). A window only helps when consecutive ranges overlap as it slides.
options: When the window size is fixed and you scan once
When many queries ask for totals of arbitrary, unrelated ranges of data that does not change
When you need the maximum of each window

questions.q: A past day's revenue is corrected after the prefix array was built. What does the update cost?
questions.explain: Prefix sums suit static data. For frequent updates and queries, Fenwick trees or segment trees do both in O(log n).
options: O(n): every prefix after that day includes it and must change

questions.q: Why does "shrink while the total is too big" fail on net cash flows that can be negative?
questions.explain: Use prefix sums with a Map of earlier prefix sums: a range from i to j has the target total exactly when prefix[i] = prefix[j + 1] − target.
options: Because negative numbers cannot be added
It assumes a bigger window never has a smaller total; with negative values, adding a day can lower the total, so dropping the left edge may discard a valid range
Because Maps cannot store negative numbers

questions.q: Why does countPeriods start its Map with 0 → 1?
questions.explain: A period from day 0 to day j has total prefix[j + 1] − 0. Without the initial 0 entry, those periods would be missed.
options: It stands for the empty prefix before day 0, so periods that start on the very first day are counted

questions.q: Why can't a running maximum be updated like a running total when a day leaves the window?
questions.explain: Sums are invertible (subtract what leaves); maximums are not. The decreasing deque keeps exactly the candidates that could become the maximum later.
options: Because maximums are always at the left edge
If the leaving day was the maximum, you cannot "subtract" it to learn the next best; that information is gone unless you kept candidates
It can; just subtract the leaving value

questions.q: In the window-maximum deque, a new day with revenue 90 arrives and the back of the deque holds a day with 75. Why is the 75 day removed for good?
questions.explain: Each position is pushed once and popped at most once, which makes the whole algorithm O(n).
options: Because the deque has a size limit
The 90 day is newer, so it stays in the window at least as long as the 75 day; the 75 day can never be the maximum again
It is not removed; both stay

questions.q: Which SQL computes a 7-row rolling revenue total inside the database?
questions.explain: Window functions are the database's sliding window. ROWS counts rows; use a date RANGE if days can be missing.
options: SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)

questions.q: For "the longest valid window" you shrink while the window is invalid. For "the shortest window whose total reaches ₦1,000,000" (non-negative revenues), when do you shrink?
questions.explain: For "shortest", every valid window is a candidate and the goal is to make it smaller, so you shrink while the rule still holds. For "longest", you shrink only to repair a broken rule.
options: Only when the window is invalid
While the window is still valid: record its length, then drop the left day to try a shorter one
Only at the end of the list

questions.q: A rate limiter allows 100 requests per user in any 60-second period. Which idea is it built on?
questions.explain: Old requests leave the window as time passes, just as old days leave a 7-day window. Limiters keep either the timestamps in the window (exact) or counts per time bucket (approximate, less memory).
options: A frequency counter over the whole day
A sliding window over time: count only the requests whose timestamps fall inside the last 60 seconds

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 6 values and a window of 3 give 4 windows: 4+2+7 = 13, then −4+1 = 10, −2+8 = 16, −7+3 = 12.

questions.q: This version subtracts the wrong day. What does it print?
questions.explain: It subtracts a day that is still inside the window (2, then 7, then 1), so the totals drift away from the truth. Trace right − k, the day that just left, on a tiny case to catch this.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: With no lates allowed, the best run is the last three. With one late allowed, positions 2 to 7 (T T F T T T) give 6; any longer window contains both lates.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: "abc" is the longest part of "abcabcbb" without a repeat; "bbbb" allows only one letter; "abba" allows "ab" or "ba", length 2.

questions.q: The same function without the prev >= left check. What does it print for "abba"?
questions.explain: At the last a, left jumps back from 2 to 1, and the window "bba" (length 3) is counted although it repeats b. The stale entry check prevents this.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: prefix[4] − prefix[1] is positions 1 to 3: 3 + 8 + 2 = 13. prefix[5] − prefix[3] is positions 3 and 4: 2 + 6 = 8.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Zero-sum periods in [1, −1, 1, −1]: positions 0–1, 1–2, 2–3 and 0–3, so 4. Periods summing to 3 in [2, 3, −3, 3]: [3], [3] (the last one) and [3, −3, 3], so 3.

questions.q: The Map starts empty instead of with 0 → 1. What does this print?
questions.explain: The correct answer is 2: [5] and [1, 4]. The period [5] starts on the first day, and only the missing empty-prefix entry could have counted it, so this version finds only [1, 4].

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Windows of 3 over 7 values: 5 windows. Their maximums are 4 (3,1,4), 4 (1,4,1), 5 (4,1,5), 9 (1,5,9) and 9 (5,9,2).

questions.q: Print the highest total of any 7 consecutive days, using a fixed-size sliding window (no nested loops). Print null if there are fewer than 7 days.
questions.explain: Fill the first window once, then add the entering day and subtract the leaving one. The best window is positions 3 to 9: 10 + 90 + 30 + 60 + 80 + 40 + 100 = 410.

questions.q: Print the length of the longest streak of deliveries with at most maxLate late ones (false), using a variable window.
questions.explain: Grow on the right, shrink on the left while too many lates are inside, and record the length. With one late allowed, the best is positions 6 to 10 (T T T F T), length 5. With two, positions 2 to 8 (T T F F T T T), length 7.

questions.q: Print the length of the longest block of consecutive ad slots in which no ad repeats. Use a variable window with a Map of last positions.
questions.explain: GLO, MTN, PEAK, DANGOTE (positions 1 to 4) and MTN, PEAK, DANGOTE, GLO (positions 2 to 5) both have 4 distinct ads; any 5 consecutive slots contain a repeat.

questions.q: Build a prefix-sum array once, then answer each query [from, to] (inclusive positions) with one subtraction. Print the answers joined with spaces.
questions.explain: O(n) to build, O(1) per query: prefix[to + 1] − prefix[from]. The leading 0 handles ranges starting at position 0.

questions.q: Count the periods of consecutive days whose net cash flow sums to exactly 0. Values can be negative, so use prefix sums with a Map of how often each prefix sum has appeared.
questions.explain: With target 0, a period ends here exactly when an earlier prefix sum equals the current one. The prefix sums are 0, 4, 0, 2, 0, 4, 0. Every pair of equal prefix sums marks one zero-sum period: the value 0 appears 4 times (6 pairs), 4 appears twice (1 pair) and 2 once (no pair), so 7 periods.

questions.q: Revenues are never negative. Print the length of the shortest run of consecutive days whose total reaches at least the target, or 0 if none does.
questions.explain: For "shortest", shrink while the window is still valid, recording its length each time. 5 + 2 = 7 takes two days. This shrinking is only safe because values are never negative.

questions.q: Print the 3-day moving average (rounded to whole naira) for each day from the third on, in O(n).
questions.explain: Keep one running total: add the new day, subtract the day that left, and divide only when producing an output. (300 + 600 + 900) / 3 = 600, (600 + 900 + 300) / 3 = 600, (900 + 300 + 1200) / 3 = 800.

questions.q: For each window of 3 days, print the highest single-day revenue, in O(n), using a deque of positions (an array with a head index is fine).
questions.explain: The deque keeps positions with decreasing revenue; the front is the maximum and is dropped once it slides out. Each position enters and leaves once: O(n).
